PHSCS 587

Intrinsic density and mass action

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows why shifting the equilibrium Fermi level trades electrons for holes

A bandgap suppresses thermally excited carriers, while available states and thermal occupation determine how many remain. For nondegenerate equilibrium carriers, n = NC exp[−(EC − EF)/(kBT)] and p = NV exp[−(EF − EV)/(kBT)]. NC and NV are effective densities of states with units of concentration, not dopant concentrations.

Multiplying the two formulas eliminates EF: np = NCNV exp[−Eg/(kBT)] = ni². Thus ni = √(NCNV)exp[−Eg/(2kBT)] is the intrinsic concentration, with n = p = ni in a pure equilibrium bulk. For a single isotropic parabolic conduction band, NC = gs gv[md kBT/(2πℏ²)]^(3/2), provided the degeneracy factors have not already been absorbed into md.

At fixed material and temperature, increasing equilibrium electron population decreases hole population according to p = ni²/n. Temperature changes both effective DOS and the gap-dependent exponential, so ni must be recomputed. Under injection, separate quasi-Fermi levels can replace the equilibrium mass-action relation; under degeneracy, full Fermi integrals replace the Boltzmann formulas.

Example

For a hypothetical semiconductor at one fixed temperature with ni = 4 × 10⁹ cm⁻³ and n = 8 × 10¹⁴ cm⁻³, the nondegenerate equilibrium model gives p = 2 × 10⁴ cm⁻³.

Practice

1. At fixed temperature, what happens to p when equilibrium n triples?

Use the constant product.

Within the nondegenerate equilibrium model, p becomes one third of its original value because np = ni².
